formulaCard.title: Income Statement Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Gross Profit} = \text{Net Sales} - \text{Cost of Goods Sold}$$ $$\text{Net Income} = \text{Gross Profit} - \text{Operating Expenses}$$

explanation: The [[kw:income statement]] (profit and loss statement) reports a company's financial performance over a specific period.
It follows: $$\text{Revenue} - \text{Expenses} = \text{Net Income (or Loss)}$$.
[[kw:Revenue]] is the amount earned from sales; [[kw:expenses]] are costs incurred to generate that revenue.
Key subtotals: Gross Profit = Revenue – Cost of Goods Sold; Net Income = Gross Profit – Operating Expenses.
[[imp:The income statement covers a period of time, unlike the balance sheet which is a snapshot.]]

explanation: [[kw:Operating expenses]] are costs incurred to run the business that are not directly tied to production.

Gross profit – Operating expenses = Net income (or Operating income if no other items).
If operating expenses exceed gross profit, the company incurs an operating loss.

blocks.title: 4. Vertical Analysis of the Income Statement

explanation: [[kw:Vertical analysis]] of the income statement expresses each line item as a percentage of net sales.
$$\text{Percent of Sales} = \frac{\text{Line Item}}{\text{Net Sales}} \times 100$$.
This reveals the cost structure: how much of each dollar goes to COGS, operating expenses, and profit.
Common benchmarks: COGS % (should be low enough to cover other expenses), net profit margin.
[[imp:Comparing these percentages over time or with competitors highlights inefficiencies.]]

notes: All other items are compared to this base.

challengeCorner.prompt: A company has net sales $1,000,000, COGS $600,000, operating expenses $250,000. Compute the vertical percentages for COGS, gross profit, operating expenses, and net income.

discoveryHook.scenario: To see how much of each sales dollar goes to different costs, we use [[kw:vertical analysis]]. In Mool Company, COGS of $180,000 is ($180,000 ÷ $320,000) × 100 = 56.25% of net sales. Operating expenses are 28.1%, leaving 15.6% as net income. This breakdown helps identify cost control issues.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The sum of percentages below net sales does not add to 100%—only the top line is 100%. [[imp:Do not expect the column to total 100; each item is independent.]]

hints: Gross profit increased from 160k to 180k; net income went from 60k to 65k, an 8.3% increase.

discoveryHook.scenario: Mool Company's net sales grew from $280,000 to $320,000 — a 14.3% increase. But operating expenses jumped from $70,000 to $90,000, a 28.6% increase. The blueprint helps spot that expenses are growing faster than sales, which may squeeze future profits.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Percent changes can be misleading for small base numbers. [[imp:A 100% increase from $1 to $2 is dramatic in percent but tiny in dollars. Always consider both dollar and percent changes.]]

blocks.title: 5. Horizontal Analysis of the Income Statement and Blueprint Aid
teacherCues: Show horizontal analysis for income statement: compare two years' income statements.
Use the blueprint to organize the calculation.

explanation: [[kw:Horizontal analysis]] of the income statement compares line items across two periods, showing dollar and percent changes.
Formula: $$\text{Percent Change} = \frac{\text{New} - \text{Old}}{\text{Old}} \times 100$$.
Apply the blueprint: Understand (which items and periods), Solve (compute dollar and percent changes), Conclude (interpret trends — are revenues growing? expenses controlled?).
Look for large percent changes that may require explanation.
[[imp:If expenses grow faster than sales, profit margins shrink.]]

notes: If the old amount is zero, percent change is not meaningful.
